body: Considering comment on https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/103025, should we always use `get_global_transform_interpolated()` instead of `get_global_transform()` in the animatable class in the C++ @lawnjelly?

> Considering comment on https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/103025, should we always use get_global_transform_interpolated() instead of get_global_transform() in the animatable class in the C++ @lawnjelly?

Generally:
* If you are doing things on the physics tick, everything should just work (this should be the preferred method for most stuff when using FTI)
* If you are doing things per frame, sometimes you have to turn off FTI for that branch (e.g. parallax backgrounds)
* If you are grabbing the xform of something physics interpolated per frame, you usually will want to use `get_global_transform_interpolated()`

Skeletons tend to be an interesting case here, as they sometimes do things per frame, and sometimes per tick (and can be switchable in the inspector), so often have to be handled on a case by case basis.

If something is moving at e.g. 5tps, and you call `get_global_transform()`, it will just judder every 1/5th of a second rather than move smoothly. Once someone realises how FTI works under the hood with previous and current xforms, this should be more obvious.

Interestingly, in the long distant past we did consider making `get_global_transform()` just pass through to be `get_global_transform_interpolated()` (and maybe having a second call like `get_global_transform_uninterpolated()` or similar for the old, or have a default bool parameter to indicate whether to return interpolated or non-interpolated).

It is one of those "damned if you do, damned if you don't" situations though. It had the potential to break existing complex code (as well as making existing code potentially slower) versus fixing up old cases that needed to use the `interpolated` version (as this issue finds). Although it is something that could potentially be revisited at some stage.

Hello, I tested the changes and it fixes the stutter, but makes the bone behaviour frame dependant, the bones move more at lower fps and move less at higher fps, please make sure that this doesn't happen because it makes the spring bone unusable again.

> Hello, I tested the changes and it fixes the stutter, but makes the bone behaviour frame dependant, the bones move more at lower fps and move less at higher fps, please make sure that this doesn't happen because it makes the spring bone unusable again.

@Kekitopu As I've already said in https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/103229, that is SpringBone's [specification](https://github.com/vrm-c/vrm-specification/blob/master/specification/VRMC_springBone-1.0/README.md); It is only mentioned in relation to the difference from the frame, and no mention is made of behavior dependent on delta. There may be ways to improve it, but at the very least, it would be treated as an enhancement rather than a bug.

A quick idea that comes to mind is defining a baseline FPS and normalizing movement values by delta, which should mitigate some differences, though eliminating them entirely is probably impossible. For example, you imagine if a 0->1->0 movement occurs at 60 FPS, the accumulated movement becomes 2. But if it become 30 FPS and that movement is observed as 0->0, the accumulated movement will be 0 no matter what we consider.

Therefore, it is impossible to emulate high FPS behavior completely in low FPS environment. While emulating low FPS in high FPS environment might be possible by some methods which we mentioned in https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/103229#issuecomment-2692606379 and https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/11904, implementing this on the user side would require complex code, so we would likely provide a solution for that purpose if there is much demand.

When I set the fps = physics tick or when I move the character in _process it looks smooth

I'd think the proper fix for this would be to add a physics process callback mode to `SkeletonModifier3D`, no? You'd need it for deterministic gameplay anyway if you have limbs that influence gameplay (such as a moving turret that fires projectiles based on bone position).
